processes.description: A round starts when someone announces or asks for changed reference details: a new phone, pager or extension, a name to use on email lists, or a counterparty's new scheduling coordinator ID, contract number, meter, pooling point or DUNS number. Schedulers and the risk group also ask desks for lists such as working customer lists, org region codes or book contacts, and forward them to whoever keeps the reference. Recipients update address books, contact sheets and counterparty records; follow-ups fix a wrong attachment or confirm what was asked.
steps: A staff member or counterparty announces a changed contact detail or counterparty identifier, or a coordinator asks desks for their current contact or customer list.
The notice or compiled list is forwarded to the schedulers, risk and settlement staff who rely on it.
Recipients update their address books, contact sheets and distribution lists.
Where a counterparty ID, contract number, meter or pooling point changed, the record is corrected in the scheduling and contract systems.
A follow-up reply resends a correct file or confirms the detail when the first message was wrong or unclear.

stalls.summary: A counterparty's contact update went out with an empty spreadsheet and had to be resent before anyone could use it.
A requester first said the answer missed the question, then wrote back that the original answer was right after all, adding a round of mail for no change.
Distribution lists drift out of date: mail failed to reach a person because the list carried the wrong form of his name, and others asked to be taken off lists.

contradictions.summary: Instructions on the same person's list entry conflict: one notice says 'Bill Williams III' must appear in the address box or he does not get the mail, while a later one asks lists to read 'Bill Williams' and not 'Bill Williams III'.

automation.approach: Keep one shared contact and counterparty register with a change log, fed by a standard change-notice form that records the counterparty, the field changed (scheduling coordinator ID, contract number, meter, pooling point, DUNS number, phone), old and new values, the effective date and the systems to update. A periodic check compares the register with the scheduling and contract systems and flags records still holding the old value; list requests go out from the register so desks confirm entries rather than retype them.
automation.rationale: Most rounds pass a single change along by forward, and the repetitive part is each recipient retyping it while lists drift out of date. A fixed change-notice layout and one register give everyone the same values and a record of when they changed; people still confirm changes with the counterparty and decide which systems are affected.

work_estimate.rationale: Many rounds show only a new phone number or name passing through, where the hands-on work is updating an address book or contact sheet in a few minutes. Rounds that change a scheduling coordinator ID, contract number, pooling points or DUNS number also need the counterparty record corrected in scheduling and contract systems, and list requests need a desk to compile its customers or region codes, which pushes some rounds toward 25 minutes. A typical round is about 8 minutes; the retyping and cross-checking is what a register and change form could take over.

processes.description: Darron Giron tells the risk contacts, by a one-line email sent the same evening, that an amount is being taken to Schedule C, removed from it, or released. A later notice can reverse or add to an earlier one, as when an amount put on Schedule C on a Friday was removed after the weekend, or when more was released the night after a first release. Each notice states only the action and the amount; the readers send nothing back in the mail.
steps: The risk group decides to put an amount on, remove it from, or release it from Schedule C for that night.
Darron Giron emails the risk contacts the action and the amount.
When a later decision reverses or adds to an earlier entry, a follow-up notice refers back to it.

automation.approach: A fixed notice template with fields for the action (add, remove, release), the amount, the night it takes effect and a reference to any earlier entry it changes, ideally filled from the record where the Schedule C entry is made so the amount is not retyped.
automation.rationale: The notices are short, alike and come from one person; a template keeps wording and amounts consistent and makes reversals traceable to the entry they change, while the decision to move amounts stays with risk management.

processes.description: Managers in the logistics and risk groups ask for headcount or a rotating analyst, write or edit the job posting, and send it to HR or recruiting staff. Candidates come by referral, internal transfer or the analyst pool; resumes are forwarded to hiring managers, an interview panel is named and a schedule sent, and interviewers return feedback. Managers also justify replacements to their superiors, confirm buy-in before candidates are contacted, write recommendation letters, and tell candidates when plans change.
steps: A manager requests headcount or an analyst for the group, with a justification where a superior asks for one.
The opening is described or posted, and HR or the analyst program is asked for candidates.
Resumes from referrals, internal candidates and the analyst pool are forwarded to the hiring managers.
Managers confirm which candidates to pursue and name the interview panel.
Interviews are scheduled and the schedule is sent to interviewers and candidates.
Interviewers give feedback and the group decides whom to bring in.
HR is told to start the hire, or candidates are told of a change in plans.

stalls.summary: Interviews are cancelled or moved when an interviewer is unexpectedly out of the office, so the slots have to be rearranged.
Feedback on candidates waits until every panel interview is done.
Staffing requests are routed to different HR contacts depending on the job, and managers wait for HR to call back.
Approval gates add a round of back-and-forth: a superior asks for justification before replacements are hired, and buy-in is sought before candidates are contacted.
Openings shift after they are announced: a posting is edited to say the role may be temporary, and later candidates have to be told of a change in plans.
Placement of an analyst stalls in a tug-of-war between two managers who each want him in their group.

contradictions.summary: Two groups claim the same analyst: Darron Giron says he understands why the other manager wants him but will not give him up unless forced, answers the other side's push with a remark about playing hardball, and proposes meeting the candidates to see where each fits better.

automation.approach: A hiring checklist each round follows: justification and approval, posting text from a standard layout, the HR contact for the job type, candidate source, interview panel, a shared interview calendar, a feedback deadline and the candidate notice. A calendar tool could offer slots across the panel and rebook cancellations, and feedback could be gathered through one form per candidate.
automation.rationale: Rounds repeat the same steps but stall on cancelled interviews, late feedback, approvals and unclear HR routing; a checklist makes each hand-off and its owner explicit. Interviewing and the hiring decision stay with managers, so only scheduling, posting text and notices lend themselves to tooling.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work per round is reviewing resumes, drafting or editing a posting, arranging an interview schedule, sitting in interviews and writing feedback or a justification. Many rounds are a single referral or posting handed to HR, a short task near 20 minutes; rounds with a named panel and an interview schedule take several interviewers' time, up to 180 minutes. A typical round is about 60 minutes. Scheduling, posting text and candidate notices could be templated or tooled; interviewing and judging candidates stay with people.
